title: Life Process

toc.title: 5.2 Sexual reproduction in plants: flower, pollination and fertilisation
5.3 Sexual reproduction in animals: internal and external fertilisation
5.4 The seed: structure, germination and dispersal
5.5 Growth, nutrition and respiration in living beings

html:
Every organism can produce young ones of its own kind. Flowering plants form seeds in their flowers, and the seeds grow into new plants. Many plants also grow directly from a root, stem or leaf. Lower plants and fungi form special units called spores. In higher animals, males and females form gametes, and the joining of the gametes starts a new life that is born from the mother or hatched from an egg. Without reproduction a species would die out. This unit studies asexual and sexual reproduction, pollination and fertilisation, the seed and its germination, and the basic life processes of nutrition, respiration and growth.

What this unit asks of you

Define reproduction and give its importance; describe fission, budding, fragmentation, regeneration, sporulation and parthenogenesis; explain natural and artificial vegetative propagation (cutting, layering, gootee, grafting, tissue culture); label a flower; explain self- and cross-pollination and double fertilisation; compare internal and external fertilisation; describe the parts of a seed, its dispersal and germination and the factors needed for germination.

5.1 Reproduction: asexual and sexual

Reproduction

Reproduction is the biological process by which organisms give birth to young ones of their own kind.

Importance of reproduction: (a) it continues the generation and prevents extinction; (b) it balances the death rate by new births; (c) it is the basis of new generations; (d) it keeps the biodiversity of the ecosystem in balance.

There are two kinds of reproduction. In sexual reproduction a male gamete and a female gamete fuse. In asexual reproduction a new organism forms from a single parent without the fusion of gametes.

5.1.1 Types of asexual reproduction

Type What happens Examples
Fission the parent cell splits; the parent no longer exists. Binary fission: into two (lengthwise or crosswise). Multiple fission: into many binary: amoeba, paramecium, euglena, bacteria; multiple: Plasmodium, Chlamydomonas
Budding a small bud grows on the body, develops into a complete organism and separates yeast, hydra, corals, jellyfish
Fragmentation the body breaks into pieces and each piece grows into a new organism Spirogyra, Marchantia, lichens, Mucor
Regeneration a cut piece of the body grows into a whole organism; the parent also regrows the lost part hydra, planaria, starfish
Sporulation single-celled spores form inside a sporangium, are spread by wind and grow into new plants in moist places fern, moss, mushroom, Mucor
Parthenogenesis a new individual develops from an unfertilised egg drone (male) honey bees, aphids, some ants

In some plants such as banana, pineapple and some cucumbers, the ovary grows into a fruit without fertilisation, giving seedless fruit. This is called parthenocarpy.

Features of asexual reproduction: no gametes are formed or fused; there is no male or female; it can start from any vegetative (body) cell; and the offspring are genetically identical to the parent (clones).

5.1.2 Vegetative propagation

The flower is the reproductive part of a plant; the root, stem and leaf are vegetative parts. Asexual reproduction from a vegetative part is called vegetative propagation.

Natural vegetative propagation

Part How it gives a new plant Examples
Root buds on roots, or food-storing roots, give new shoots sweet potato, dahlia, asparagus, guava, sissoo
Underground stem: sucker shoots grow from the base of the main stem banana, bamboo, mint
Underground stem: rhizome flat, food-storing stem with buds ginger, turmeric, bojho
Underground stem: corm swollen base of the shoot with a few buds pindalu (colocasia), gladiolus
Underground stem: bulb round stem with fleshy leaves and buds onion, garlic, tulip
Underground stem: tuber swollen stem with eyes (buds) potato, yam
Aerial stem buds at the nodes grow roots and shoots sugarcane, dubo grass
Bulbils small buds that drop and grow agave (ketuke), lily, pineapple
Leaf buds in the notches of the leaf margin Bryophyllum (pattharchatta), begonia, snake plant

Artificial vegetative propagation is producing new plants asexually with tools and techniques to improve the quality and quantity of crops.

  1. Cutting — pieces of stem, root or leaf are planted; a stem cutting should be from a one-year-old twig and have at least two nodes. Rose, sugarcane, lemon.
  2. Layering — a low, soft branch (the layer) has 2–3 cm of bark removed, is bent and buried in moist soil; when roots form it is cut off and planted. Jasmine, grape.
  3. Gootee (air layering) — a ring of 2–3 cm of bark is removed from a branch at least a year old, covered with moist soil (with manure or hormone) and wrapped in plastic; after one to two months roots form and the branch is cut and planted. Litchi, mango, guava, orange, pomelo.
  4. Grafting — two closely related plants are joined. The rooted lower part is the stock (a year-old seedling cut 20–30 cm above the ground); the shoot of a high-quality plant is the scion. Their cut surfaces are fitted, bound with grafting tape and wax so no air enters, and kept in shade. The new plant gives fruit of the scion's quality. The Nepal Agricultural Research Council (NARC) produces many grafted fruit plants.
  5. Tissue culture — a tiny piece of the parent plant (explant) is grown in a nutrient medium (culture medium) with hormones in a sterile laboratory; it forms a mass of cells called callus, which grows into thousands of disease-free plantlets. It is the most advanced method.

Advantages of artificial propagation: the variety can be chosen; plants bear fruit early; many identical plants are produced quickly; plants without viable seeds (banana, sugarcane) can be multiplied.

Layering Grafting
a branch roots while still attached to the parent two parts of different plants are joined
only one plant is involved stock and scion from two related plants
gives a copy of the same plant combines a strong root with a good-quality shoot

5.2 Sexual reproduction in plants: flower, pollination and fertilisation

Sexual reproduction is reproduction by the fusion of male and female gametes of the same species. The fused cell is the zygote, which grows into the new organism. Organisms with only male or only female organs are unisexual; those with both (e.g. the mustard flower, earthworm) are bisexual (hermaphrodite).

Features: gametes form and fuse; male and female organs exist; offspring show variation, are more adaptable to a changing environment and make evolution possible.

5.2.1 The flower

The flower is the reproductive part of a flowering plant.

Whorl Part Function
Calyx (sepals) green outer leaves protects the flower in the bud
Corolla (petals) coloured leaves attracts insects and birds
Androecium (stamens) filament and anther; pollen grains form in the anther male part
Gynoecium (pistil) stigma, style, ovary with ovules female part

5.2.2 Pollination

Pollination

Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or of another flower of the same species.

A pollen grain is a single, microscopic cell with a double wall; its sticky or rough outer wall helps it stick to the stigma.

Self-pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma of the same flower (autogamy) or of another flower on the same plant (geitonogamy). It occurs in small, dull flowers without nectar or scent. Paddy, wheat, groundnut, pea. Advantages: good parental characters are kept; seed formation is almost sure; no agent needed. Disadvantages: no new characters; reproductive vigour slowly falls; bad characters cannot be removed.

Cross-pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species. It occurs in colourful, scented flowers with nectar, or where anther and stigma ripen at different times. It needs agents:

Agent Name Examples
wind anemophily maize, pine, mango
water hydrophily Vallisneria, some water plants
insects (bee, butterfly, fly) entomophily mustard, sunflower, pumpkin
birds (sunbird, tailorbird) ornithophily bottle-brush, silk cotton

Advantages: new and better varieties; offspring adapt better; seeds germinate well. Disadvantages: depends on agents; good characters may not be preserved; unwanted characters may come in.

5.2.3 Fertilisation and double fertilisation

Fertilisation

Fertilisation is the fusion of a male gamete with a female gamete (egg) of the same species to form a zygote.

In a flowering plant: (1) a pollen grain on the stigma absorbs water and sugar from the stigma fluid and grows a pollen tube; (2) the tube grows down through the style into the ovary and enters an ovule; (3) on the way its nucleus divides to form two male gametes; (4) one male gamete fuses with the egg → zygote (becomes the embryo); (5) the other fuses with the secondary nucleus (the two fused polar nuclei) → endosperm nucleus (becomes food store). Because two fusions happen, this is double fertilisation; it is found only in flowering plants.

After fertilisation, the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit; the petals, stamens, style and stigma usually wither.

Pollination Fertilisation
transfer of pollen from anther to stigma fusion of male gamete and egg
happens on the stigma, outside the ovary happens inside the ovule (in the ovary)
needs agents in cross-pollination needs a pollen tube
comes first follows pollination

5.3 Sexual reproduction in animals: internal and external fertilisation

In most animals males and females are separate. The male's testes produce sperms; the female's ovaries produce ova (eggs). Forming gametes is called gametogenesis. A sperm has an oval head, a middle piece and a long tail for swimming; an ovum is much larger and round, with stored food. Millions of sperms are made, but in a woman usually only one ovum is released in a month.

During fertilisation only one sperm enters the ovum, and their nuclei fuse to form the zygote — the first cell of the new individual. The zygote divides to form an embryo, which grows into a baby. The time from fertilisation to birth or hatching is the embryonic (gestation) period.

Male → sperm, female → ovum → (fertilisation) → zygote → embryo → young one

Internal fertilisation External fertilisation
sperm and ovum fuse inside the female's body (in humans, in the fallopian tube) sperm and ova fuse outside, in water
mating is needed the female lays many eggs; the male sheds sperms over them
fewer eggs, well protected very many eggs, many are eaten or lost
insects, reptiles, birds, mammals (human, cow, bat, whale, pigeon, tortoise, butterfly) fish and most amphibians (frog)

Internal fertilisation is safer because the gametes and embryo are protected from drying, temperature change and predators inside the female's body.

Classify the fertilisation

Question. Name the type of fertilisation: human, pigeon, tortoise, butterfly, fish, bat, frog, cow, dragonfly, whale.

Answer. Internal: human, pigeon, tortoise, butterfly, bat, cow, dragonfly, whale. External: fish, frog.

5.4 The seed: structure, germination and dispersal

After fertilisation the zygote in the ovule develops into an embryo, and the ovule becomes a seed that can grow into a new plant under suitable conditions.

5.4.1 Structure of a seed

  1. Seed coat — outer covering of two layers: thick outer testa and thin inner tegmen. It protects the seed and keeps it dormant in bad conditions.
  2. Embryo — the living baby plant: radicle (becomes the root), plumule (becomes the shoot) and cotyledons (seed leaves). Cotyledons protect the radicle and plumule, store food in dicots, and in many plants come above the soil as the first green leaves. Monocots have one cotyledon, dicots two.
  3. Endosperm — stored food (starch, protein) used by the embryo until the seedling can make its own food. All monocot seeds (maize, rice) have it; most dicot seeds (bean, pea, gram) store food in the cotyledons instead.

5.4.2 Dispersal of seeds

Dispersal is the carrying of seeds away from the parent plant by an agent. It reduces crowding and competition and lets the plant reach new places.

Agent Features of seed/fruit Examples
Wind small, light, with hairs, wings or air sacs (lower density, so they float in air) silk cotton (simal), aak, kans and khar grass, dandelion, maple
Water light, waterproof, can float lotus, coconut, mangrove
Animals edible fleshy fruits (seeds swallowed and passed out, or thrown away); hooks and spines that stick to fur jamun, kafal, guava, harro, amala; kuro (cobbler's pegs), bhede kuro
Gravity heavy fruits fall below the plant mango, apple, coconut
Bursting of pods dry pods burst and throw seeds out mustard, pea, bean, sesame, gram, dhaturo

5.4.3 Germination

Germination and dormancy

Germination is the development of the root and shoot of a new plant from a seed. Dormancy is the resting state in which a dry seed stays alive without growing; it preserves the life and germinating power of the seed until conditions are suitable.

When a seed gets water, air and warmth, it swells and its enzymes become active. The radicle comes out first and grows down into the root; then the plumule grows up into the shoot; the cotyledons may become the first green leaves.

Factors needed for germination

Factor Why it is needed
Water softens the seed coat, breaks dormancy, starts metabolism (seeds are soaked about 24 hours before sowing)
Air (oxygen) for respiration in mitochondria, which releases energy for growth
Suitable temperature about 16–24 °C for most seeds; very high or low temperature stops it
Light not needed by most seeds to sprout, but the seedling needs it to photosynthesise
Germination percentage

Problem. A farmer tests 50 wheat seeds on moist cotton; 42 germinate. Find the germination percentage. Is the seed good for sowing if at least 80 % is needed? Solution. Germination % =\frac{42}{50}\times100\%=84\%. Yes — 84 % is more than 80 %.

Activity 5.13 — three seeds on one stick

Tie three similar seeds on a stick — one at the top, one in the middle and one at the bottom — and stand it in a beaker so that the bottom seed is under water, the middle one half in water and the top one in air. After 2–3 days only the middle seed germinates: the top seed has air but no water, the bottom seed has water but too little air. Conclusion: both water and air are needed.

Importance of germination: continues the plant's generation; good germination increases farm yield; germinated seeds (sprouts) are more nutritious; germination of grass and tree seeds conserves forests and pastures.

The case of Suryanarayan's wheat field

Situation. Suryanarayan sowed wheat and dug the field again to bury the seeds. Seedlings were good in the moist part but poor in the dry part.

Answers. (i) He dug again to cover the seeds with soil so that they get moisture and warmth and are not eaten by birds. (ii) In the dry part there was not enough water to break dormancy. (iii) Irrigate the field evenly (or sow after rain), use good seeds, and sow at the right depth and season.

5.5 Growth, nutrition and respiration in living beings

Nutrition is taking in and using food. Green plants are autotrophs: they make their own food by photosynthesis in chloroplasts:

carbon dioxide + water --(sunlight, chlorophyll)--> glucose + oxygen

Animals, fungi and most bacteria are heterotrophs: they depend on food made by others, either by eating it (holozoic, e.g. cow, human), absorbing it from dead matter (saprophytic, e.g. mushroom) or living on a host (parasitic, e.g. tapeworm).

Respiration is the breakdown of food (glucose) in the cells to release energy. It happens in the mitochondria of all living cells, day and night:

glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

Without oxygen (anaerobic respiration), yeast makes alcohol and carbon dioxide, and tired muscles make lactic acid; much less energy is released.

Growth is the permanent increase in the size and mass of an organism, caused by cell division and enlargement. It uses the food from nutrition and the energy from respiration. Plants grow throughout life at their tips (meristems); animals grow until adulthood.

Process Experiment that shows it Result
Photosynthesis needs light destarch a plant, cover part of a leaf, test with iodine covered part stays brown; the rest turns blue-black
Photosynthesis releases oxygen Hydrilla under a funnel and test tube in water, in sunlight gas relights a glowing splint
Respiration releases CO₂ breathe through lime water lime water turns milky
Germinating seeds respire seeds in a flask with lime water lime water turns milky

Chapter summary

  • Reproduction gives birth to one's own kind; it is asexual (no gametes) or sexual (fusion of gametes).
  • Asexual types: fission, budding, fragmentation, regeneration, sporulation, parthenogenesis. Offspring are identical to the parent.
  • Vegetative propagation: natural (root, sucker, rhizome, corm, bulb, tuber, aerial stem, bulbil, leaf) and artificial (cutting, layering, gootee, grafting, tissue culture).
  • Flower: sepals, petals, stamens (anther + filament), pistil (stigma + style + ovary).
  • Pollination: self (autogamy, geitonogamy) and cross (wind, water, insects, birds).
  • Double fertilisation: male gamete + egg → zygote; male gamete + secondary nucleus → endosperm. Ovule → seed; ovary → fruit.
  • Animals: internal fertilisation (insects, reptiles, birds, mammals) and external (fish, frog).
  • Seed = seed coat + embryo (radicle, plumule, cotyledons) + endosperm; dispersed by wind, water, animals, gravity and bursting; germinates with water, air and warmth.

14. (d).

Group B — Short answer (2 marks each)

  1. Differentiate:(a) fission and budding(b) bulbil and rhizome(c) natural and artificial vegetative propagation. [3]
  2. Give reasons:(a) Asexual reproduction has no concept of male and female.(b) Growing potatoes from tubers is vegetative propagation.(c) Farmers benefit from grafting.(d) Tissue culture is the most advanced method of vegetative propagation. [4]
  3. Name the method of asexual reproduction: yeast, paramecium, pineapple, banana, planaria, begonia, ginger, onion, sugarcane, Mucor, sweet potato, Spirogyra. [3]
  4. What are stock and scion? Write two advantages of grafting. [2]
  5. Differentiate:(a) gamete and zygote(b) anther and pollen grain(c) autogamy and geitonogamy. [3]
  6. Give reasons:(a) Pollinating agents play a great role in pollination.(b) Both male and female are needed for sexual reproduction.(c) Internal fertilisation is safer than external fertilisation. [3]
  7. What is gametogenesis? Where does it occur in plants and animals? [2]
  8. Differentiate:(a) dispersal and germination of seeds(b) plumule and radicle(c) dispersal of mustard seeds and of kafal seeds. [3]
  9. Give reasons:(a) Seeds germinate if soaked in water.(b) Silk cotton seeds are dispersed far.(c) Eating sprouted seeds is more beneficial than dry seeds. [3]
Answers to Group B

1. (a) In fission the parent splits and disappears (amoeba); in budding a bud grows on the parent and separates, and the parent remains (yeast, hydra). (b) A bulbil is a small bud that falls and grows (agave, lily); a rhizome is a thick underground stem with buds lying flat under the soil (ginger). (c) Natural propagation happens by itself through roots, stems or leaves (potato, Bryophyllum); artificial propagation is done by people with tools (cutting, layering, grafting, tissue culture) to improve crops.

2. (a) There is no formation or fusion of gametes; only one parent is involved. (b) The tuber is a stem (a vegetative part) and its eyes are buds that grow into new plants. (c) Grafted plants bear fruit early and have the high quality of the scion, so yield and income increase. (d) Thousands of disease-free, identical plantlets are produced from a tiny piece in a short time in any season.

3. Yeast — budding; paramecium — binary fission; pineapple — bulbils (and suckers); banana — sucker; planaria — regeneration; begonia — leaf; ginger — rhizome; onion — bulb; sugarcane — stem cutting (aerial stem); Mucor — sporulation (and fragmentation); sweet potato — root; Spirogyra — fragmentation.

4. The stock is the lower rooted part (a young seedling); the scion is the twig of a good-quality plant joined on it. Advantages: early fruiting; fruit of the desired quality; combines a hardy root with a productive shoot.

5. (a) A gamete is a single reproductive cell (sperm or ovum); a zygote is the cell formed by fusion of two gametes. (b) The anther is the part of the stamen that makes pollen; a pollen grain is the tiny cell formed in it that carries the male gametes. (c) Autogamy: pollen to the stigma of the same flower; geitonogamy: pollen to another flower of the same plant.

6. (a) In cross-pollination pollen cannot move by itself; wind, water, insects and birds carry it. (b) The male gives the sperm and the female the ovum; only their fusion forms the zygote. (c) The gametes and embryo stay inside the female's body, protected from drying, cold and predators.

7. Gametogenesis is the formation of gametes. In plants it occurs in the anther (pollen, male gametes) and ovule (egg); in animals in the testes (sperms) and ovaries (ova).

8. (a) Dispersal is carrying seeds away from the parent; germination is the growth of a seed into a seedling. (b) The plumule grows upward into the shoot; the radicle grows downward into the root. (c) Mustard seeds are thrown out when dry pods burst; kafal seeds are swallowed by birds and animals with the fruit and passed out elsewhere.

9. (a) Water softens the coat, breaks dormancy and starts enzyme action. (b) They are light and covered with silky hairs, so the wind carries them. (c) Sprouting changes stored food into simpler forms and increases vitamins, so sprouts are easier to digest and more nutritious.

Group C — Long answer (4 marks each)

  1. What are the types of asexual reproduction? Describe budding in hydra with a diagram. [4]
  2. Compare self-pollination and cross-pollination with their advantages and disadvantages. [4]
  3. What is double fertilisation? Describe the process. [4]
  4. Write the methods of seed dispersal and explain any one with examples. Name the method for mango, chestnut, maple, gram, cobbler's pegs, sesame, pumpkin, coconut and pear. [4]
  5. Explain the germination of a seed with a diagram, and the role of air in germination. [4]
  6. "If there is no pollination, fertilisation is nearly impossible." Justify. What happens if the style of a flower is removed? [4]
Answers to Group C

1. Fission, budding, fragmentation, regeneration, sporulation, parthenogenesis. Budding in hydra: when food is plenty, a small bulge (bud) appears on the side of the body; it grows, develops a mouth and tentacles, and finally separates as a new hydra. Draw the stages as in the figure in 5.1.1.

2. Self: pollen to the same flower or same plant; small dull flowers; no agent needed; seed setting is sure and parent characters are kept, but no new variety and vigour falls. Cross: pollen to another plant of the same species; bright, scented flowers with nectar; needs agents; gives new, stronger and better-adapted varieties, but depends on agents and may bring unwanted characters.

3. Two fusions in the ovule of a flowering plant. The pollen grain forms a pollen tube that grows through the style to the ovule; its nucleus forms two male gametes; one fuses with the egg to form the zygote (→ embryo) and the other fuses with the secondary nucleus to form the endosperm nucleus (→ endosperm). Then the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary the fruit.

4. Wind, water, animals, gravity and bursting of pods (table in 5.4.2). Mango — gravity (and animals); chestnut — bursting/gravity; maple — wind; gram — bursting of pods; cobbler's pegs — animals (sticking); sesame — bursting of pods; pumpkin — animals/people; coconut — water; pear — animals.

5. The seed absorbs water and swells, the coat softens, enzymes change stored food into simple sugar, the radicle emerges and grows down, then the plumule grows up and the cotyledons open as the first leaves (draw a bean seedling with seed coat, radicle, plumule and cotyledons). Air gives oxygen for respiration, which releases the energy needed for cell division and growth; seeds in waterlogged soil fail for lack of oxygen.

6. Fertilisation needs the male gametes, which reach the ovule only in a pollen tube that grows from pollen lying on the stigma; without pollination no pollen reaches the stigma, so no pollen tube, no male gamete and no fertilisation (except in parthenocarpic fruits, which have no seeds). If the style is removed, the stigma is also lost and the pollen tube has no path to the ovary, so fertilisation and seed formation cannot occur.
